extracted.intended_audience: ACL'23 reviewers and authors (novice and experienced conference reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for performing and writing peer reviews for ACL'23 (and similar NLP conferences), including reviewer qualification checks, conflict-of-interest rules, reading strategy, author response handling, and discussion participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of assignment information
rubrics_metrics.description: All the information about submissions and reviews that you receive as part of your assignment is confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you participate in discussions of peer review on social media, make comments general enough that no submissions can be identified and the authors cannot identify you. Do not refer to individual papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide accurate reviewer profile for matching
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that you have provided all the information about you which the venue asked for (sign-up forms, reviewer profiles, Semantic Scholar profile).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This information is used for computing conflicts of interest and paper-reviewer assignments. For ACL 2023, the semantic scholar field is set through softconf global profile; accurate profile increases likelihood of getting papers in your area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check qualification to review ('Am I qualified to review this?')
rubrics_metrics.description: After receiving an assignment, skim the paper to check whether this is something that you are qualified to review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's normal to be asked to review papers a bit outside your subfield as long as you're familiar with the core methodology. If your expertise does not cover certain aspects, explicitly state that in the review and indicate your confidence score in the review form. Less-than-perfect matches can be useful for cross-field exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest and anonymity checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether you know or can guess who the authors are and whether anonymity is preserved; assess personal and academic conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If anonymity is not preserved, contact your chair/action editor — the paper should be desk-rejected. If you know the authors from personal communication/social media/talks, ask for re-assignment. For submissions impossible to anonymize (e.g., 'too famous'), indicate your awareness of the authors’ identity in the review form. Recuse yourself for close academic conflicts (e.g., work very close to your own).

rubrics_metrics.name: Desk-reject conditions (style/page-limit/anonymity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers that do not follow style guides, go over the page limit, or break anonymity can be desk-rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page limit does not include the ethical considerations section. If you think the paper should be desk-rejected for these reasons, contact your chair or action editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan your time / submit early
rubrics_metrics.description: Block time in your calendar to work on the review and submit it on time, preferably a few days before the deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate time by average reading + writing time; participating in forum discussion may add time. Novice reviewers submitting early gives area chairs time to catch grave issues. Avoid doing reviewing in a single session; write a draft and revisit it later to reduce knee-jerk reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid first-pass commenting; read for contribution type
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not heavily annotate or comment during the very first read. First skim to understand the overall type of contribution and the framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenting during first read can bias you toward a prototypical paper in your area and against other contribution types (resource papers, analysis, reproduction, surveys, negative results). Judge the study for what it is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental-paper reading order (intro/method before results)
rubrics_metrics.description: For experimental papers, avoid looking at the results when first skimming; read the introduction and methodology before results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pause and ask: is the research question clear? Would the methods answer it? Do you want to know the answer? Will the answer advance the field? This focuses evaluation on the knowledge gained rather than on whether results are 'positive'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust expectations by paper length/type
rubrics_metrics.description: Note whether the paper is long or short and adjust expectations accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long papers are expected to describe completed work with thorough evaluation and analysis. Short papers may present proof-of-concept or a convincing point and are not expected to have extensive evaluation — only minimal but convincing evidence for the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious when looking up references to avoid de-anonymization
rubrics_metrics.description: Looking up references or concurrent work can reveal non-anonymous preprints and accidentally discover the authors' identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform lookups cautiously to avoid opening yourself to social biases caused by knowing the authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-aware writing (authors, other reviewers, AC, SAC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about who will read your review: authors, other reviewers, the area chair (AC), and the senior area chair (SAC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors need clear, actionable instructions to improve the paper; they will not see discussion. Other reviewers should be engaged — your review can open doors for discussion. AC needs specific, self-contained reviews to write meta-reviews and will not have time to read the paper closely. SAC will calibrate across papers; reviews should be self-contained to place the paper in the pool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give actionable, specific feedback (not vague comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make suggestions that give authors a clear path to improvement rather than vague statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'not enough experiments' is less actionable than 'the results would be stronger with validation on the LDC NYT dataset.' If new information arises in discussion, modify your review so authors get all relevant information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make reviews self-contained for area chairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Write reviews so that area chairs can understand the main issues without re-reading the paper in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACs and SACs may not read the paper closely, so include sufficient context and specificity to make their job of writing metareviews and calibrating easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author response purpose and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of the author response period is to make sure reviewers understand the paper correctly and to state how authors will address easy-to-fix issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reviewers misunderstood claims, indicate where claims are stated. If requested changes are easy camera-ready fixes, state how you'll address them. ACL'23 disallows reporting new experimental results in the rebuttal — consider whether newly performed results are necessary to back up claims (a weakness) or are nice-to-have (a suggestion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag policy violations in author rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: If you received a review that violates conference policies, indicate this in the rebuttal form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should point out policy violations during rebuttal so meta-reviewers can take them into account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participate in discussion period
rubrics_metrics.description: After author responses, reviewers should take part in discussion, especially when scores vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion is to catch mistakes, misunderstandings, or policy violations and to exchange opinions. It's an opportunity to learn and to update your review; edit your review if new relevant information appears in discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors should respond to reviews (even negative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are encouraged to respond to reviews even when they are very negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At minimum, thank the reviewers. If reviews found serious issues, treat them as help to improve; if reviews misunderstood the paper, use rebuttal to clarify. Pointing out policy violations strengthens peer review norms. Responses are read by reviewers and chairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of reviewer variance and implicit biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that variance in reviewer experience, different understandings of evaluation criteria, and implicit social/academic biases can affect judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting popularity of task, language, engineering vs linguistic focus, or fame of lab unduly influence evaluation. Be explicit about what you consider a 'weakness' (fundamental flaw vs lack of clarification/experiment) and how different weaknesses should affect recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate confidence and expertise limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: If your expertise does not cover certain aspects of the submission, specify that and use the confidence score in the review form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being explicit about limits of expertise helps area chairs interpret your review and helps other reviewers know which parts of the paper you were best positioned to judge.
